L2t: Murder can be established by extreme-indifference recklessness, where a person consciously disregards a very high risk to human life, without any intent to kill.
L3t: Knowingly delivering an anticancer drug he had been told was well below strength, to protect contracts, could let a jury find extreme recklessness, and the defect need not be the only cause of death, since it hastened the death.
L4t: The conviction should stand, because a jury could find that knowingly shipping the sub-strength drug was reckless enough to count as murder and that it caused the earlier death.
L2f: Federal drug-safety laws set labeling and potency standards for medicines and are enforced mainly through inspections, recalls and fines.
L3f: Murder requires proof that the defendant intended to kill, and a manufacturer who ships a substandard lot for business reasons is violating a product-quality rule, not acting with homicidal intent.
L4f: The conviction must be reversed, because shipping the defective lot was merely a regulatory offense and cannot support a murder conviction.
cand_true: No, a jury could find reckless conduct sufficient for murder
cand_wrong1: Yes, it was only a regulatory offense
cand_wrong2: Yes, because the patient would have died soon anyway, so there was no causation
